Response to your questions:

1. The output requirement is based on system losses, what size film, energy density requirement of the film for short pulse, oversized illumination fields etc. With certain film, 1 joule is very workable, but also much lower can be used in the right circumstances. 

2. If the light you refer to is not the input beam, but the optical pumping, safety generally refers to heat deposit and thermal stress fractures. That depends on many factors. 3. Okay now I'm confused, pump light, did you mean input beam? 

4. It will work but only allow you to achieve a very small energy output. For 1 joule, nd:glass large aperture(3/8 or 1/2 inch) to keep beam energy density down so you don't pit your rod ends, burn AR coatings.

5. Nothing wrong with rotating q switches they work. more of a mechanical wear alignment issue. Cr4+:yag passive q switches are nice but you have limited output energy range with a specific fixed crystal absorption density as compared to liquid dyes concentrations. But the best part is crystal q switches have no maintenance requirements!

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
The power you get is related to the losses of the system, the gain of the medium, the pump rate, the length of the gain medium and the cross section of the rod. It is quite possible to get very large gains in a MOPA. Since the output of the resonator is quite low (about 20mj or so) it takes a good amount of gain to get real power. With 6mm dia 63mm long Nd:YAG I calculated I can get about 300mj of energy from each stage.

first stage: 20 mj

second stage: 320mj

third stage 620mj

As you can see you only get x amount from a given volume of gain material. In practice you will not extract all of the energy from the second stage unless you pass the beam back through the amplifiers making 4 stages out of the second two stages. This is achieved with polarizing beam splitters and waveplates.

Amplifier: 20mj

Isolator

Beam Splitter

Second stage: 170 mj

Third Stage: 450 mj

1/4 waveplate

mirror

Third Stage backwards: 470mj

Second Stage backwards: 620 mj

Since all of these extra components are quite expensive the frugal holographer will just add another stage. Ron Olsen has a great idea of replacing the third stage with Nd:Glass. Nd:YAG has very high gain limiting the useful length to about 60mm. (Beyond that the spontaneous emission starts to deplete energy from the rod and contaminate the beam.)

Nd:Glass on the other hand has a very low gain making it possible to make a amplifier that has Joules of gain in a single stage. Nd:Glass has a very broad florescent line making it unsuitable for a resonator but it works well as an amplifier.

posts.author: Ron Michael
posts.content_md:
There are a lot of issues with amplification.

Here is a few things that come to my mind.

guess this could be a holowiki entry:

1. The gain medium's emission cross section [http://www.rp-photonics.com/cross_sections.html](http://www.rp-photonics.com/cross_sections.html) relates to the pumping and energy storage leveling off (population inversion level) achieveable. Once gain reaches the physical conditions ripe for ASE, the depopulation increases and the gain levels off. The larger the emission cross section the lower the useful storage to be extracted. This can be modulated by temperature for example, cooling ruby and heating nd:yag will allow more extraction.

2. input beam energy density and power level also play a role in extraction efficiency and output level. optimum j/cm2 increases extraction which gives higher output.

3. signal gain is also related to rod length. The more amplifer length the higher the output. Additionally higher gain can be had from many short rods well spaced apart than from one long rod. (ASE related)

4. small signal gain is exponential compared to larger signals regarding amplification. 

5. amplication of q switch pulses is different. Generally much less output due to optical pump time is much longer than signal time. after the signal all pump energy is wasted.

Let me demonstrate point 4 and 5: 

Below is a test where the variables like pump time etc were not changed.

medium is Nd:yag. 

multiple q switch output (9 to 11 pulses) for duration of pump time 140usec:

19mj oscillator, 488mj output from amps. 25x increase

single pulse 2/3 time interval of pump time:

3mj osc, 183mj amp. 61x

double pulse 

6.5mj osc, 244mj amp. 32x

In the first case these were multiple 2 mj pulses. 

So for a single pulse only 3mj extracted from the oscillator, most of the energy was wasted. 

in the second case notice "small signal"gain is much higher compared to the third case 61x compared to 32x.

posts.author: ron olson
posts.content_md:
To whom amplification may concern:

The issue with Nd:Glass is not so much gain related as it is medium related. Nd:YAG is a difficult crystal to grow in large boules - the Neodymium atom is replacing a smaller aluminum atom and this doping distorts the crystal making large boules very expensive and of dubious optical qulaity. Nd:Silicate glass (as used for Nd:YAG amplification) is cheap to pour and doping levels of 2-3% result in amplifiers that introduce very few detrimental effects in the beam and fewer losses in the pocketbook. Because the glass has less gain than YAG, the chances for spontaneous emission (and thus gain depletion) are reduced along with the need for anti-reflection rod coatings. Nd:YAG's chief attributes are narrow bandwidth (good for SLM oscillators); high gain and good thermal conductivity (good for high average power amplifiers). Keep in mind that what you gain financially in a cheaper glass rod, you pay back in-part with increased demands on the power supply (capacitors are expensive in their own right) but if your goal is to produce a single-shot, high energy beam with the best possible beam quality - I believe Nd:Glass is your best option.

posts.content_md:
Ron,

You make some good points about Yag and Glass but obtaining higher output is also related to some of my earlier points on laser medium's inherent characteristics. Extractable energy is basically Est*area where Est energy storage density in j/cm2. small signal gain is exp(Est/Esat) where Esat is photon energy/emission cross section. So Esat for Yag is 1.82E-19/6.5E-19 or about 0.28 j/cm2. For Q-246 nd:silicate it would be 1.82E-19/2.9E-20 or about 6.28j/cm2 Since gain is related to Est/Esat and if Est is much greater than Esat the high gain causes ASE to become a problem, If Est is much lower than Esat then system losses are a problem. So for efficiency Est closer to Esat is preferred. This means that for a given gain of say 2.718 = exp(est/esat) where est and esat are the same, (I'm normalizing this) then for nd:yag Est is .28j/cm2 and nd:glass is 6.28j/cm2. Going back to extractable energy given a fixed area of rod size then nd:glass is storing more energy that can be extracted as useful energy. I hope that helps

> **Hans:** - What is the definition of Est and Esat?

Est = Energy Storage Density in J/cm^2

To calculate this it would be easiest to reference Section 4.1 of Solid State Laser Engineering by Koechner.

Esat = photon energy/emission cross section

> **Hans:** - Is it really possible to replace only the amplifier nd:YAG rod with a nd:Glass rod?

Yes. 

> **Hans:** I thought that nd:Glass lases at 1054nm and nd:YAG at 1064nm.

To find out what frequency you can get a material to lase at you look at the fluorescent lines. Nd:Glass has a very wide line that includes 1064nm. The problem is it is so wide (over 27nm!) that making a SLM oscillator out of it would be difficult.

posts.author: Ron Michael
posts.content_md:
Watch out for the phosphate glasses. You want the efficiency peak near your desired wavelength.

Kigre Nd:silicate Q-246 is okay [http://www.kigre.com/glass.html](http://www.kigre.com/glass.html)

You can rework the formulas for volume instead of area but values like

Esat Saturation Fluence (Koechner chapter 4.1 formula 4.8 refers to it as Es) which are based on emission cross section in cm squared give rise to units canceling properly. Extractable E = Est*area is (j/cm2) * cm2 losing the cm2. Esat is hv/(gamma*sigma) where gamma is 1 for a 4 level system and sigma is the emission cross section in cm2 so Esta is J/cm2 

then gain is exp(Est/Esat) or (j/cm2)/(j/cm2) or dimensional-less value.

posts.author: Ron Michael
posts.content_md:
Hans,

Work your system from the goal back to the design.

You indicated you wanted 1 joule output. 

You have at least two choices Ruby or Nd/SHG

Nd/SHG due to conversion efficiency requires high output prior to conversion. Ruby offers high output without conversion and now more film and plates are available for it. Years ago,I would not have recommended to others due to the lack of plates available for it. Today it should not be discounted. I have for years made portraits without the waxy look.

Lets say you decide you prefer Nd/SHG laser. 

-Calc the beam size based on efficient SHG conversion.

-Watch your damage limits.

-Assume 25 to 50 percent conversion. (worse case).

that indicates a need for up to 4 joule laser for 1 joule 532 output (worse case). Remember Ron Olson indicated work with 250mj output was okay for the film he tested with. He suggested a 1joule/250mj system.

-based on beam size and damage limits and output prior to conversion, pick you amplifiers (Nd:glass with possible combination of nd:yag)

-Nd:glass like Ruby will require anywhere from 1500j to 6000j pump depending or cavity design and rod size. 

-Water cooled amplifiers tend to be more efficient that aircooled ones due to fresnel reflections are greatly eliminated by the water and less thermal deposit since water absorbs longer IR.

-Zenon is the lamp of choice. you will need several for large amps. (some designs have use 2 to 6 of the linears lamps).

1 joule 532 output is going to be expensive since you have to have large enough rods and SHG crystal. The larger KDP etc tend to be less efficient so you should design around the 25% conversion just to be sure.

1 joule ruby is less expensive since 3/8 inch rods can do the job and no conversion is needed. My last ruby versions 8 and 9 showed good efficiency at 6kj total input compared to my version 7 which as air cooled system used 24Kjoules of flashlamp power and large rods. These systems generated 1 to 2.5 joules of power. Just go to the website if you are curious.

Actually it is okay to start small budget, find your rods and lamps first, get a good price on a SHG. Buy yourself some test equipment, work a few projects for experience. Then with that you will eventually get the system you want. Or find a deal on surplus system and modify it.

Hans,

A good rule of thumb is not to exceed 10j/cm2 of energy density and best to keep it closer to 5j/cm2 for coating issues. This is based on typical q switch lasers of the 5 to 20ns levels. The shorter the pulse the higher the peak power and the damage threshold is reduced. Also when ordering optics make sure they also can handle this as well. So 4 joules averaged in 1 cm2 would be a good target. The Peak gaussian ouput is 2x this or 8j/cm2. So watch out for peak energy as well. This density indicates a minimum of 1 cm2 rod area. But don't forget diffraction effects and the rule of thumb there is 2x the required diameter for typical gaussian beam profiles. This would indicate about a 1/2 inch rod diameter which if nd glass and would require typical 5000 joules for a 6 inch long rod for example. Also this gives you some room incase you encounter more negative thermal lensing than you expected on the final amplifier. The use of a SBS conjugate mirror of course helps to correct some of these issues but also single pass systems also are holographic but thermal lensing muste be considered. I agree Koechner just compiles the references into his book and you do have to work through these formulas and other sited references. But you will find all this and more regarding the design of solid state systems. Some will just have to be learned the hard way or work with others who have successfully designed a system like the individuals you referenced.

posts.author: doug694
posts.content_md:
This response is primarily for Hans (assuming its not too late - he might have finished his project already 

I wanted to mention that there are lots of areas worth consideration if you are worrying about expense in a laser project.

Optics can be _incredibly_ expensive and really awkward to source, especially when you start looking at mirrors and etalons. For a first pulsed laser project, it is definitely worth considering a route which will not lead you to an expensive dead-end when you need that all-important component later on.

I have found sourcing YAG optics is relatively cheap and easy (particularly HR mirrors, windows, prisms and q-switches) since they are abundant in industry and usable ones are retired from service regularly. 

KTP crystals are also relatively common although they always sell quickly and can sometimes be pricey. YAG rods are common but tend to be expensive - often exponentially with respect to rod size! 

Surplus/ebay rods are often damaged and useless even when the seller states otherwise (you can't repair them, in case you are wondering - its _way_ too expensive - I have had quotes before!) so unless you are sure of what you are getting it is perhaps wise to avoid non-trusted sources for rods.

As an example: I have a wonderful 10mm x 150mm yag rod which I got from a trashed laser, but it has a tiny pit on one end which makes it practically useless for anything other than blowing holes in stuff (and it probably wouldn't last long doing that). I inquired about repair costs for this (and other salvaged, bargain & freebie rods) which resulted in alarming responses. A minimum of $400 to refurbish a 50mm yag rod! I won't even mention the quote I got on the 10mm x 150mm rod (I hope this deters people trying to pick up 'repolishable' crystals on ebay).

Ruby rods and optics are comparable with YAG cost-wise, potentially cheaper but usually harder to source due to limited applications. Ruby is now nearly redundant in industry. Most of the optics I have found were at a good price, but ireally nteresting parts (like partial mirrors with known R%) appear so rarely. The only reliable source seems to be those military tank laser heads which are still around (but even they are getting more scarce) and retired medical lasers - although some have rods with integral mirrors which limits their usefulness.

You can also expect a difference in cost for capacitors intended for a ruby or yag laser. Ruby lasers tend to need a big bank of capacitors, but the capacitor profile is not as demanding as YAG - the pulse forming time is longer. The electrolytics I used in my first ruby laser were common photoflash types and worked ok. The maxwell capacitors I used for YAG were difficult to obtain and expensive, and if I had tried to match the electrical storage of the ruby laser it would have been _prohibitive_.

If you pick an exotic gain medium (however cheaply you might source it) with an unusual emission line for your oscillator, you could have problems getting the necessary optics. Some mirrors have very narrow wavelength response - for instance yag mirrors coated for 1320nm will allow most of the 1064 to pass in order to prevent 1064 becoming dominant. If you are forced to pick'n'mix optics you have a better chance of success with common, matched components than exotic or poorly documented ones.

My point really is, depending on what you decide upon early in your design, you could end up with disproportionate expense later on when you need to add something specific. By sticking to common materials you'll have a better chance of initial success, then you can start incorporating more unusual designs incrementally with a better chance of understanding the implications of each change, and hopefully with less expense.

Doug
